description: Explorer at heart. I started out in design and found my way into consulting and strategic product development. I bring UX, service design, visual storytelling and human-centered thinking to complex problems, and I love turning technology and data into experiences people can understand and use.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator transforms complex lunar data into an interactive decision-support experience. Instead of asking users to interpret separate datasets and technical tools, the prototype lets them explore the Moon directly, select candidate landing areas, move through time, and see how sunlight, direct-to-Earth communication, terrain, and periods of darkness change.

Users define mission priorities, explore candidate sites near the lunar south pole, test different landing dates, and pin promising scenarios for comparison. The goal is not to recommend a “safe” landing site, but to make the trade-offs behind a possible landing window easier to see, understand, and explore.

The mission profiles (solar rover, science lander and comms outpost) are illustrative examples. In a real mission, engineers would enter their own power, battery and communication requirements, and the tool then shows which sites and dates meet them.

The concept combines NASA lunar terrain data with astronomical calculations, scientific visualization, interactive storytelling, and a generative ambient soundtrack to turn lunar mission data from something users inspect into something they can experience. Its sunlight and Earth-visibility results closely match NASA’s own illumination maps (r = 0.99 and 0.98).

Don’t just browse lunar data. Explore the decision.
details:
The problem

Planning a lunar mission is not only about choosing a location. Conditions change with both place and time. Sunlight affects available solar power, direct visibility of Earth affects communication opportunities, and local terrain can alter when the Sun or Earth disappears below the horizon.

The challenge is therefore not just access to data. It is helping people understand the relationship between these conditions well enough to compare possible mission scenarios.


The concept

Lunar Landing Site Navigator turns this into a five-step interactive journey:
Explore → Target → Timing → Evaluate → Pin & Compare

Users first choose a mission profile with different example requirements for power, Earth communication, and periods without sunlight. They then explore the lunar south pole directly on a 3D Moon and select a candidate landing area.

By changing the landing date, users can see how mission conditions change over time. The prototype visualizes sunlight, direct-to-Earth visibility, periods where both are available, and local horizon effects.


From data to decisions

Rather than presenting a single “best” landing location, the prototype allows users to pin different site/date combinations and compare the trade-offs.

A mission-fit score provides a simplified way of comparing scenarios against the selected example criteria. It is a decision-support and educational device, not a NASA recommendation or complete landing-safety assessment.


Design and storytelling

The Moon itself is the primary interface. Instead of placing lunar data inside a conventional dashboard, users navigate the geography directly and experience how conditions change.

The experience also includes generative ambient music that changes with each step of the journey. Sound is used as an additional layer of scientific storytelling rather than as a replacement for visual information. The interface has been designed with accessibility in mind, including readable contrast, redundant visual labels, and interactive information that does not rely on color or sound alone.


Potential impact

The concept shows how complex scientific and space data can become more accessible through human-centered design. The same principles could support mission planners, educators, students, and space enthusiasts in exploring the relationships between lunar geography, time, illumination, and communication.

With further development, the prototype could incorporate additional mission constraints and higher-fidelity scientific modelling while preserving the central idea: helping users understand the reasoning behind a mission decision instead of simply presenting more data.

Use of AI

The application’s code, data processing and interface design were developed with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic), directed, tested and reviewed by me. The background music is generated live in the browser by code. The demo video is a real screen capture of the app, assembled with AI-assisted scripts and marked “AI-assisted production”; the voice-over is my own recorded voice. No AI-generated images and no NASA logos or branding are used.

Source code: https://github.com/birgit-ct/lunar-landing-site-navigator, released under the Apache 2.0 licence.
